title: Information Retrieval
text: Information retrieval (IR) is the activity of obtaining information system resources relevant to an information need from a collection. Web search engines are the most visible IR applications. A query does not uniquely identify a single object; several objects may match with different degrees of relevancy. Precision is relevant retrieved divided by total retrieved. Recall is relevant retrieved divided by total relevant. The inverted index maps terms to documents containing them. Boolean retrieval uses set intersection and union. Ranked retrieval orders documents by relevance score.

title: TF-IDF Ranking
text: TF-IDF stands for term frequency-inverse document frequency. It reflects how important a word is to a document in a corpus. TF-IDF value increases proportionally to the number of times a word appears in the document and is offset by the number of documents in the corpus that contain the word. This adjusts for words that appear frequently in general. It is one of the most popular term-weighting schemes used in information retrieval and text mining for document ranking and keyword extraction.

title: PageRank Algorithm
text: PageRank is an algorithm used by Google Search to rank web pages. It was named after Larry Page of Google. PageRank works by counting the number and quality of links to a page to estimate its importance. More important websites receive more links from other websites. The algorithm outputs a probability distribution representing the likelihood that a random link-clicker arrives at any particular page. PageRank uses a damping factor alpha of 0.85 and iterates until convergence. It is a foundational algorithm in web information retrieval.

title: Machine Learning
text: Machine learning (ML) is a field of inquiry devoted to understanding and building methods that learn from data to improve performance on tasks. It is part of artificial intelligence. Machine learning algorithms build a model based on sample training data to make predictions without being explicitly programmed. Applications include email filtering, speech recognition, computer vision, and recommendation systems. Supervised learning uses labelled data. Unsupervised learning finds patterns in unlabelled data. Reinforcement learning learns through rewards and penalties.

title: Natural Language Processing
text: Natural language processing (NLP) is a subfield of linguistics, computer science, and artificial intelligence concerned with the interactions between computers and human language. Goals include text classification, machine translation, sentiment analysis, named entity recognition, question answering, and text summarization. NLP uses techniques from computational linguistics, machine learning, and deep learning. Tokenization splits text into tokens. Stemming reduces words to their root form. Lemmatization maps words to their canonical form using a vocabulary and morphological analysis.

title: Search Engine
text: A web search engine is a software system that is designed to carry out web searches. They search the World Wide Web in a systematic way for particular information specified in a textual web search query. The search results are generally presented in a line of results, often referred to as search engine results pages. Information may be a mix of links to web pages, images, videos, infographics, articles, and other types of files. Search engines also maintain real-time information by running an algorithm on a web crawler. The most popular search engine is Google followed by Microsoft Bing and Yahoo.

title: Recommender System
text: A recommender system is a subclass of information filtering system that seeks to predict the rating or preference a user would give to an item. Content-based filtering uses item features to recommend similar items the user has liked. Collaborative filtering uses ratings from many users to find similar users and recommend items they liked. Hybrid systems combine both approaches. Matrix factorization decomposes the user-item rating matrix into latent factors. Cosine similarity measures the angle between two vectors and is widely used in both content-based and collaborative recommendation systems.

title: Web Crawling
text: A web crawler is an internet bot that systematically browses the World Wide Web, typically for the purpose of web indexing. Web crawlers can copy pages for processing by a search engine, which indexes the downloaded pages so users can search more efficiently. Crawlers consume resources on visited systems and often visit sites without permission. Duplicate detection prevents re-crawling the same page. Politeness policies respect robots.txt files. Breadth-first crawling visits pages level by level from seed URLs. Focused crawlers target specific topics or domains.

title: Inverted Index
text: An inverted index is an index data structure storing a mapping from content, such as words or numbers, to its locations in a database file, or in a document or a set of documents. The purpose of an inverted index is to allow fast full-text searches, at a cost of increased processing when a document is added to the database. The inverted file may be the database file itself, rather than its index. It is the most popular data structure used in document retrieval systems, used on a large scale in search engines like Google, Bing, and Yahoo. Each term in the vocabulary maps to a posting list of document IDs.

title: HITS Algorithm
text: Hyperlink-Induced Topic Search (HITS) is a link analysis algorithm that rates web pages. It was developed by Jon Kleinberg. The algorithm identifies two types of web pages: hubs and authorities. Authorities are pages that contain useful information on a topic. Hubs are pages that link to many authorities. A good hub is a page that links to many authorities. A good authority is a page that many hubs link to. The algorithm is iterative and updates hub and authority scores alternately until convergence. HITS and PageRank are the two most well-known link analysis algorithms used in web information retrieval.

title: Text Mining
text: Text mining, also referred to as text data mining, is the process of deriving high-quality information from text. It involves the discovery by computer of new, previously unknown information, by automatically extracting information from different written resources. Text mining uses methods from information retrieval, information extraction, machine learning, statistics, and computational linguistics. Common tasks include text classification, clustering, concept or entity extraction, production of granular taxonomies, sentiment analysis, document summarization, and entity relation modeling. Feature extraction transforms raw text into numerical feature vectors using approaches like bag-of-words or TF-IDF.

title: Precision and Recall
text: Precision and recall are two evaluation metrics for information retrieval systems. Precision is the fraction of retrieved documents that are relevant. Recall is the fraction of relevant documents that are retrieved. There is often a tradeoff between precision and recall. Increasing recall typically decreases precision and vice versa. The F1 score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall. Average precision summarizes a precision-recall curve as the weighted mean of precisions achieved at each threshold. Mean average precision (MAP) is the mean of average precisions across multiple queries. NDCG measures ranking quality with graded relevance judgments.

title: Neural Networks
text: A neural network is a network or circuit of neurons or in a modern sense an artificial neural network composed of artificial neurons or nodes. Thus a neural network is either a biological neural network made up of biological neurons, or an artificial neural network for solving artificial intelligence problems. Artificial neural networks are used for deep learning, which is a subset of machine learning. Deep learning uses multiple layers of neural networks to learn representations of data. Convolutional neural networks are used for image recognition. Recurrent neural networks are used for sequential data like text and speech.

title: Cosine Similarity
text: Cosine similarity is a metric used to measure how similar two documents are irrespective of their size. Mathematically, it measures the cosine of the angle between two vectors projected in a multi-dimensional space. The cosine similarity is advantageous because even if the two similar documents are far apart by the Euclidean distance, they could still be oriented closer together. The smaller the angle, the higher the cosine similarity. In information retrieval, each document is represented as a vector of TF-IDF weights, and cosine similarity computes the angle between query and document vectors. Values range from 0 (orthogonal, no similarity) to 1 (identical direction).

title: Boolean Retrieval
text: The Boolean model of information retrieval is a classical information retrieval model and represents the simplest model to use. The Boolean model treats each document as a set of words. Queries are Boolean expressions of keywords connected by AND, OR, and NOT operators. The model views each document as a set of index terms. AND retrieval returns documents containing all query terms. OR retrieval returns documents containing any query terms. NOT retrieval excludes documents containing specific terms. Boolean retrieval is fast due to inverted index lookups but does not provide ranking of results. Extended Boolean models add term weighting to rank results.

title: Stemming and Lemmatization
text: Stemming is the process of reducing inflected or derived words to their word stem, base or root form. A stemmer for English typically strips common suffixes like -ing, -ed, -er. The Porter Stemmer is a widely used stemmer for English that applies a series of transformation rules. Lemmatization is the process of grouping inflected forms of a word so they can be analysed as a single item, identified by the word's lemma. Unlike stemming, lemmatization uses vocabulary and morphological analysis. Lemmatization produces actual dictionary words while stemming may produce non-words. Both techniques reduce vocabulary size and improve recall in information retrieval.
